knowledgePoint.title: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form

result.markdown:
![](images/aa/aab03da9e57863ce49011b6e6d9e1cd2cb64aa4c3eabfe5f323f505074c3b987.png)

The equation $x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 6$ represents an ellipse. The normal line at the point $(\sqrt{2}, 1)$ on the ellipse intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P$. What are the coordinates of $P$?
result.solution: Implicit differentiation gives the tangent slope $-x/(4y)=-1/(2\sqrt2)$ at $(\sqrt2,1)$. The normal slope is its negative reciprocal, $2\sqrt2$. Thus the normal is $y-1=2\sqrt2(x-\sqrt2)$. Setting $y=0$ yields $$x=\sqrt2-\frac1{2\sqrt2}=\frac3{2\sqrt2}.$$ Therefore $P=(\tfrac3{2\sqrt2},0)$.
result.title: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form

The equation $3x^{2} - 2y^{2} = 4$ represents a hyperbola. The normal line at the point $(2, 2)$ on the hyperbola intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P$. What are the coordinates of $P$?
result.solution: Differentiating gives $6x-4y\,y'=0$, hence the tangent slope at $(2,2)$ is $3/2$. The normal slope is $-2/3$, so its equation is $y-2=-\tfrac23(x-2)$. At $x=0$, $y=2+\tfrac43=\tfrac{10}3$. Thus $P=(0,\tfrac{10}3)$.

knowledgePoint.title: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given a Description of the Radius and Angle

result.markdown: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1$, and that $P$ makes an angle of $\frac{5π}{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P$?
result.solution: Use $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$. With $r=1$ and $\theta=5\pi/3$, the coordinates are $(\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$.
result.title: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given a Description of the Radius and Angle

knowledgePoint.title: Finding a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector in a Diagram

result.markdown:
![](images/9d/9dfaf74a497a2fd22428e09a4c26d573e184c9728ccf67f11ebb9d6a2a44f4c6.png)

Consider the picture above. Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $q + r$?
result.solution:
The scale shows that two grid squares represent one unit. Reading the displacements from the diagram gives

$$
q=\left\langle\frac52,-\frac32\right\rangle,
\qquad r=\left\langle\frac32,3\right\rangle.
$$

Thus $q+r=\langle4,\frac32\rangle$ and

$$
|q+r|=\sqrt{4^2+\left(\frac32\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{73}}2.
$$

The required unit vector is

$$
\frac{q+r}{|q+r|}=\frac{2(q+r)}{\sqrt{73}}.
$$
result.title: Finding a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector in a Diagram

knowledgePoint.title: Differentiating a Function Using the Chain Rule and Prime Notation

result.markdown:
Given that $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-3x+3}}$, complete the expression for $f'(x)$ by entering the missing factor.

$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{(x^2-3x+3)^{3/2}}\,($ {{field-1}} $)$
result.solution:
Let $g(x)=x^2-3x+3$ and rewrite the outer function as $F(u)=2u^{-1/2}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiate the outer and inner functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F'(u)&=2\left(-\frac12\right)u^{-3/2}=-u^{-3/2}, \\
g'(x)&=2x-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=F'(g(x))g'(x) \\
&=-(x^2-3x+3)^{-3/2}(2x-3) \\
&=\frac{3-2x}{(x^2-3x+3)^{3/2}} \\
&=\frac{1}{(x^2-3x+3)^{3/2}}(3-2x).
\end{aligned}
$$

The missing factor is $3-2x$. It includes both the inner derivative and the outer derivative's factor of $-1$.

Since $x^2-3x+3=(x-\frac32)^2+\frac34>0$, this derivative is defined for every real $x$.
result.title: Differentiating a Function Using the Chain Rule and Prime Notation

knowledgePoint.title: Completing the Square on a Quadratic Expression

result.markdown: Complete the square on the quadratic expression $x^2+3x-2$.
result.solution:
Rewrite the linear coefficient with $2$ as a factor:

$$
x^2+2\cdot\frac32 x-2.
$$

Add and subtract $\left(\frac32\right)^2$ so the expression keeps the same value:

$$
\underbrace{x^2+2\cdot\frac32 x+\left(\frac32\right)^2}-\left(\frac32\right)^2-2.
$$

Factor the perfect square, then combine the constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x+\frac32\right)^2-\frac94-2
&=\left(x+\frac32\right)^2-\frac94-\frac84\\
&=\left(x+\frac32\right)^2-\frac{17}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
result.title: Completing the Square on a Quadratic Expression

knowledgePoint.title: Differentiating a Quotient of Two Polynomials

result.solution:
Let $u(x)=x^2-2x+2$ and $v(x)=x^2+x+1$. Then

$$
u'(x)=2x-2,\qquad v'(x)=2x+1.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
f'(x)=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}.
$$

Expand the two products in the numerator separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}u'(x)v(x)&=(2x-2)(x^2+x+1)\\&=2x^3+2x^2+2x-2x^2-2x-2\\&=2x^3-2,\\u(x)v'(x)&=(x^2-2x+2)(2x+1)\\&=2x^3+x^2-4x^2-2x+4x+2\\&=2x^3-3x^2+2x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract these products and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{(2x^3-2)-(2x^3-3x^2+2x+2)}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\\&=\frac{2x^3-2-2x^3+3x^2-2x-2}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\\&=\frac{3x^2-2x-4}{(x^2+x+1)^2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The cubic terms cancel. The derivative is valid for every real $x$, since $x^2+x+1=(x+\tfrac12)^2+\tfrac34>0$.
result.title: Differentiating a Quotient of Two Polynomials
